summary: Describes state machines for GIST, showing the states of nodes for a given flow and their transitions, to help in implementation. It is informational.

subtitle: Flowcharts showing every step a signaling node takes in establishing paths

tldr.problem: GIST (General Internet Signaling Transport) is a complex protocol for delivering signaling messages along network paths, and implementers need to understand the exact sequence of states and events.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides state diagrams and transition tables for querying nodes (that initiate signaling) and responding nodes (that receive it), showing which states they move through and what triggers each transition.
tldr.outcome: Implementers can use these diagrams to build working GIST code, though the RFC notes that the GIST specification itself is authoritative and implementations may achieve the same results using different approaches.

today: RFC 5972 is an Informational RFC that aids implementers of GIST (RFC 5971). It has not been obsoleted. The RFC itself notes that the GIST specification (RFC 5971) is authoritative; implementations may use different internal approaches as long as they achieve correct protocol behavior.

sections.title: What GIST Does and Why Diagrams Help
sections.content:
GIST is the transport layer for NSIS (Next Steps in Signaling), a framework for carrying signaling messages (such as resource reservation requests) along a network path from source to destination. Unlike in-band signaling protocols that rely on data flow, GIST works independently to discover the next signaling peer, establish message associations (reliable or unreliable transport connections), and forward signaling data.

The protocol involves complex message exchanges: a querying node (upstream) sends a Query to discover the next peer, the responding node (downstream) sends a Response, and a three-way handshake may require a Confirm. Parallel instances of state machines run for different flows and signaling types. The RFC provides state diagrams and transition tables to help implementers understand and code the protocol correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: GIST is how network signaling finds its way across the internet, hopping from one router or node to the next. The diagrams show the dance they do to connect.

sections.title: State Machines, Messages, and Modes
sections.content:
A GIST node can act as a querying node (initiating a discovery, asking "who is the next node?") or a responding node (answering the question). Each entity has its own state machine. A state is a condition the node is in; a transition is a move from one state to another triggered by an event (receiving a message, a timer expiring, an application request). The RFC defines common events: receiving Query, Response, Confirm, or Data messages; receiving requests from the NSLP application; timer expirations; and messaging association (MA) state changes.

GIST supports two transmission modes: D-mode (Datagram, unreliable) and C-mode (Connection-oriented, with a message association). Nodes choose modes based on local policy and NSLP application requirements. The state machines track which mode is in use, whether a message association needs establishment, and whether confirmations are required before installing state.
sections.plainLanguage: A node is either asking (querying) or answering (responding). States are like waiting rooms, and messages or timers decide which room to move to next. Nodes can send over unreliable or reliable transport, and the state machine tracks which.

sections.title: The Querying Node State Machine
sections.content:
The querying node has three main states: IDLE (waiting for an NSLP application request), Wait Response (sent a Query, waiting for a Response), Wait MA Establishment (received a Response that needs a new message association), and Established Downstream MRS (a Message Routing State is installed and signaling can flow). The state machine begins in IDLE; an application request triggers a transition to Wait Response. A Response message can lead directly to Established (if D-mode or an existing MA can be reused) or to Wait MA Establishment (if a new connection is needed).

The state machine also handles path changes, refreshes, retries when responses time out, and error conditions. If a Response times out, the Query is retried a fixed number of times before notifying the application of failure. If the responding node is new (path changed), the querying node may need to establish a new message association or reuse an existing one. Timers (T_No_Response for waiting on Response, T_Refresh_QNode for refreshing established state) drive state transitions.
sections.plainLanguage: The querying node waits for a request, sends a Query, waits for an answer, possibly sets up a connection, and then maintains the link with periodic refreshes.

sections.title: The Responding Node State Machine
sections.content:
The responding node also has states: IDLE, Wait Confirm (received a Query, waiting for a Confirm if local policy requires three-way handshake), and Established Upstream MRS. When the responding node receives a Query, it decides based on local policy whether to install the Message Routing State immediately (moving to Established) or wait for a Confirm (moving to Wait Confirm). The responding node sends a Response message with a Responder Cookie if confirmation is needed.

If the responding node is in Wait Confirm and receives a Data message before the Confirm, it detects a lost Confirm and sends a Response indicating the problem. Similarly, if a new Query arrives while waiting for Confirm, it resends the Response. Timers (T_No_Confirm, T_Expired_RNode) handle timeouts. The responding node also refreshes state when it receives new Queries from the same upstream peer, and it deletes state when the lifetime expires or the application requests it.
sections.plainLanguage: The responding node receives a request, waits for confirmation if policy demands it, and then maintains the link. If confirmation is lost, it notices and resends the Response.

sections.title: Transitions, Events, and Variables
sections.content:
Each transition in the state machines is labeled with a number and described with: (1) the triggering event (receiving a message, an application request, a timer firing, an error), (2) the actions taken (transmitting a message, starting or restarting a timer, installing or deleting state), and (3) the resulting state. The RFC provides detailed transition tables in Appendix A with entries for each state, listing all possible exit conditions.

Key variables tracked include: ConfirmRequired (whether local policy demands explicit confirmation), NewPeer (whether the responding peer has changed), MAexist (whether an existing message association can be reused), RespCookie (the responder's cookie sent in the Response), timers like T_No_Response and T_Inactive_QNode, and the stored UpstreamPeerInfo (in responding nodes). These variables condition transitions: a Response that arrives with an existing MA available takes a different path than one that requires establishing a new MA.
sections.plainLanguage: Each transition has a reason (event), a result (action), and the next state. The machine also tracks data like whether a new peer showed up, whether confirmation is needed, and if an old connection can be reused.
